title: The ablative absolute

objectives.can: Recognise an ablative absolute and translate it as a clause of time, cause, condition or concession.

explanation.summary: An ablative absolute is a noun or pronoun in the ablative with a participle (or another noun or adjective) in the ablative agreeing with it. The phrase is not tied to the rest of the sentence by case. It gives the circumstances of the main action, and the reader decides from the sense whether it means 'when', 'because', 'if' or 'although'.

sections.heading: What it is
body: In Matthew 17:5 the sentence begins *Adhuc eo loquente, ecce nubes lucida obumbravit eos*. The main clause is *nubes ... obumbravit eos*: a cloud overshadowed them. The first words, *eo loquente*, say what was going on at that moment: 'he still speaking'. *eo* is a pronoun in the ablative and *loquente* a present participle in the ablative agreeing with it.

This is the ablative absolute. 'Absolute' comes from a Latin word meaning 'loosed': the phrase is loosed from the grammar of the main clause. *eo* is not the subject of *obumbravit* (that is *nubes*), not an object, and not governed by a preposition. The ablative case is the sign of the construction, and the participle agrees with its noun in case, number and gender in the ordinary way.
English has a similar form, the absolute participle phrase: 'the doors being shut, he came'. Latin uses it far more often.

sections.heading: The participle and its time
body: The tense of the participle is relative to the main verb, as in the infinitive of indirect statement. A present participle is simultaneous with the main verb. In *Sedente autem eo super montem Oliveti, accesserunt ad eum discipuli* (Matthew 24:3), the sitting and the coming happen together: 'as he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him'.

A perfect passive participle is earlier than the main verb. In *Et his dictis præcedebat ascendens Jerosolymam* (Luke 19:28), *his dictis* means 'these things having been said': he spoke first, then went on ahead. *Hoc audito Jesus ait illis* (Mark 2:17) is 'this having been heard, Jesus said to them'. Latin has no perfect active participle for most verbs, so the passive form serves where English would say 'having heard' or 'having said'.

The verb *sum* has no present participle in the classical language. For that reason, when 'being' would be needed, the phrase can be two nouns, or a noun and an adjective, side by side in the ablative, with 'being' understood. The best-known case in this lesson is *te duce* in Augustine, 'you leading', and *te teste*, 'you being witness'.

sections.heading: How to translate it
body: The ablative absolute does not say how it is related to the main verb. The sense must decide, and the same phrase can often be read in more than one way. The usual relations are these.
Time: *Adhuc eo loquente* (Matthew 17:5), 'while he was still speaking'. Also *Facto vespere* (Matthew 16:2), 'when it is evening', literally 'evening having come about'.

Cause: *viso Domino* in John 20:20. The disciples were glad *viso Domino*: 'on seeing the Lord', which is also 'because they saw the Lord'. Time and cause shade into each other, and the Latin leaves it open.
Condition: *Deo volente* (Acts 18:21), 'God willing', that is, 'if God wills'.

Concession: *Venit Jesus januis clausis* (John 20:26). The phrase can be read 'with the doors shut', or 'although the doors were shut'. The second reading shows how the Latin is neutral and the translator chooses.

In a translation, an English subordinate clause is often better than a participle phrase. 'These things having been said' is accurate but stiff; 'when he had said this' or 'after this' is usually the right English.

sections.heading: Accompanying circumstances, and the participle that is not absolute
body: In Mark 16:20 the apostles preached *Domino cooperante et sermonem confirmante sequentibus signis*. There are three ablative phrases in a row: 'the Lord working with them, and confirming the word, with signs following'. They give the circumstances of the preaching, and none is tied to the main verb by anything but the ablative.

Compare a participle that is not absolute. In *Tunc Herodes videns quoniam illusus esset a magis, iratus est valde* (Matthew 2:16), *videns* is a nominative that agrees with *Herodes*, the subject of *iratus est*. It describes the subject and is not absolute. A participle is absolute only if its noun does not appear in the main clause as subject or object. Some phrases look nearly alike: *Hoc audito Jesus ait* has *Jesus* as subject of *ait*, but *audito* agrees with *hoc*, not with *Jesus*, so the phrase is absolute even though Jesus is the one who heard.

To find one, look for a noun or pronoun in the ablative with a participle in the ablative beside it, outside the grammar of the main verb. Ask what the phrase tells you about the circumstances, and then choose the English that fits.

misunderstandings: Thinking the noun in the ablative is the subject or object of the main verb. It stands outside the main clause: in *eo loquente* the subject of *obumbravit* is *nubes*.
Giving the perfect participle the time of the main verb. A perfect passive participle such as *dictis* or *audito* is earlier than the main verb.
Treating the translation as fixed. The Latin gives only the circumstance: time, cause, condition and concession are readings of the sense, and a phrase may allow more than one.
Calling any participle in the ablative an ablative absolute. If the participle agrees with a noun that is the subject or object of the main verb, it is an ordinary participle.

deeper.heading: The absolute that comes close to the sentence
body: A strict ablative absolute has a noun that is not in the main clause, but writers do not always keep to this. Cases like *Hoc audito Jesus ait* can be read as absolutes even though the hearer is the subject of the main verb. Some grammarians count such uses as loose or as a result of the passive participle having no active partner. The student's test is practical: is the participle tied by agreement to a noun in the main clause or not?

In the Vulgate the construction often copies a Greek genitive absolute, the similar loosened phrase of Greek. The Latin translators regularly put it into the ablative, which is why ablative absolutes are common in the Gospels and Acts.

examples.analysis: *eo loquente* is the absolute: a pronoun and a present participle in the ablative. The main clause is *nubes ... obumbravit eos*, and its subject is *nubes*, not *eo*. The present participle shows simultaneous time: 'while he was still speaking, a cloud overshadowed them'.

examples.analysis: *Sedente autem eo super montem Oliveti* is another present-participle absolute, with the pronoun *eo* between participle and preposition phrase. The main verb is *accesserunt*, and the disciples are its subject. Translate it as a time clause: 'as he sat'.

quoted.title: Mark
quoted.english: But they going forth preached every where: the Lord working withal, and confirming the word with signs that followed.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: After the main verb *prædicaverunt* come ablative phrases that give the circumstances: *Domino cooperante*, *sermonem confirmante* and *sequentibus signis*. The noun of each phrase differs from the apostles who preach. The phrases are best read as 'while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed'.

It is an absolute that gives the circumstance (means or help) of the action.

check.explain: *januis clausis* is a noun and a perfect passive participle in the ablative, outside the grammar of the main verb. It states a circumstance, and the context lets a reader hear 'although'. The doors are not the object of any verb.

options: viso Domino: 'the Lord having been seen', that is, 'on seeing the Lord' or 'because they saw him'
check.explain: *viso Domino* is the absolute: a noun and a perfect passive participle in the ablative. The subject of the main verb is *discipuli*. The participle is earlier than the rejoicing, and the phrase may be read as time or cause.

options: eo is the subject of both verbs
discipuli is the subject of accesserunt, and eo is the noun of the absolute, referring to Jesus
check.explain: In an ablative absolute the noun is outside the main clause. *discipuli* are the ones who come, and *eo* (Jesus) is the one who sits.

options: audito agrees with Hoc, not with Jesus, so the participle is not tied to the subject
check.explain: The participle is neuter ablative and agrees with *Hoc*. It does not agree with *Jesus*, which is nominative. Because Latin has a perfect passive participle but no perfect active one, 'having heard this' is expressed as 'this having been heard'.

options: An ablative absolute made of a pronoun and a noun, with 'being' understood: 'with you as leader'
A vocative with an address to the reader
check.explain: Latin has no present participle of *sum*, so a pronoun and a noun in the ablative can make an absolute without a participle. *te duce* means 'you leading', that is, 'with you as my guide'.

check.explain: *non invento corpore ejus* is the absolute: 'his body not having been found'. *dicentes* is nominative and describes the subject of *venerunt*, so it is an ordinary participle, not an absolute.
